metadata.note: The Northern Pacific Railway, the northern transcontinental chartered by Abraham Lincoln in 1864 and completed with a golden spike at Gold Creek, Montana in 1883, plus the Portland section its SP&S subsidiary carried down the Columbia Gorge. Route geometry is mostly hand-placed waypoints through the real cities on the NP main line, NOT taken from any modern Amtrak alignment and not surveyed track centerline, because no passenger train has run this corridor since 1979 - Amtrak's Empire Builder follows the rival Great Northern route further north. UPDATED: the Duluth-St. Paul segment (previously a crude 2-point straight line) has been real-traced from OpenStreetMap active-rail geometry instead; the rest of the route (St. Paul westward) remains hand-placed waypoints pending the same treatment. Era boundaries follow real, sourced milestones; headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not real timetables. REFINEMENT (2026-08-18): the main line was redrawn because long stretches were long stretches unrealistically straight. It now uses ~75 division points and station towns, following the river valleys the railroad was actually surveyed along - the Yellowstone (Glendive-Livingston), the Missouri (Three Forks-Townsend-Helena), the Clark Fork (Missoula-Paradise-Noxon) and the Yakima (Pasco-Yakima-Ellensburg) - plus the Bozeman Pass, Mullan Pass and Stampede Pass crossings. Still hand-placed town waypoints, not surveyed track centerline. The main line now carries ~125 division points and station towns following the river valleys the railroad was surveyed along - the Yellowstone (Glendive-Livingston), Missouri (Three Forks-Townsend-Helena), Clark Fork (Missoula-Sandpoint) and Yakima (Pasco-Ellensburg) - plus the Bozeman, Mullan and Stampede pass crossings. Duluth was also split out as its own feature: it was NP's original eastern terminus on a separate prong joining the St. Paul main at Staples, and including it in the same LineString had created a false ~200km straight link. Still hand-placed town waypoints, not surveyed track centerline. The Idaho panhandle portion (Clark Fork - Sandpoint - Spokane) of the main line is no longer hand-placed: it now embeds the OpenStreetMap-traced track geometry from northern_pacific_idaho_panhandle.geojson, which follows the real surveyed alignment at roughly 1.5km point spacing. That standalone file still covers the same stretch in its own right, so the two are intentionally coincident there. UPDATE (2026-08-26): the SP&S Portland Section is no longer a 6-point hand-placed sketch - it is now real-traced from OpenStreetMap over the ex-SP&S north bank line (BNSF Fallbridge and Lakeside Subdivisions), 383 points from Pasco station down the Columbia Gorge through Wishram, Bingen, Stevenson and Camas to Vancouver, across the Columbia and down the Portland peninsula to Union Station, 220.1 mi Pasco - Vancouver against a documented 221. See that feature's geometry_quality for the dam-era realignment caveat. The Seattle - Portland feature (np-tacoma-kalama-portland) is still a 6-point hand-placed sketch.

metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

segments.note: Abraham Lincoln signed the Northern Pacific's charter in 1864 for a railroad from the Great Lakes to Puget Sound, financed by Jay Cooke & Co. Work began in 1870 at Carlton, MN, and by 1873 the line ran west to Bismarck, ND, plus an isolated section from Kalama, WA to Tacoma; NP leased the St. Paul-Duluth line in 1872. The Panic of 1873 wiped out Cooke and halted construction for years. (Full Duluth-Seattle route shown regardless of the year each section opened.) estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The last spike was driven at Gold Creek, Montana, near Garrison, on Sept 8 1883 - former president Ulysses S. Grant drove the final golden spike - completing the main line from the Great Lakes to the Pacific. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The North Coast Limited entered service Apr 29 1900, running 2,228 miles Chicago-Seattle via Bismarck (the Chicago-St. Paul leg ran over connecting rails; NP's own line began at St. Paul/Duluth). It became one of the great western name trains, later famous for its Loewy-styled two-tone green livery and Vista-Dome cars. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The North Coast Limited got a faster schedule in Nov 1952, and the new Mainstreeter took over roughly its old schedule, routed via Helena. Across Montana the NP had two lines between Logan and Garrison - via Helena over Mullan Pass (the original 1883 main, and the alignment shown here) and via Butte over Homestake Pass. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: Northern Pacific merged into Burlington Northern on Mar 2 1970. The North Coast Limited made its final run Apr 30 1971, the day before Amtrak began. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: Amtrak declined to keep the North Coast Limited, but ran a similar service, the North Coast Hiawatha, over this corridor until its last run Oct 6 1979. Since then this route has had NO passenger service - Amtrak's Empire Builder uses the rival Great Northern line to the north instead (see great_northern.geojson). estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The North Coast Limited carried a Portland section that split from the Seattle section at Pasco, WA and ran down the north bank of the Columbia River Gorge over NP subsidiary the Spokane, Portland & Seattle Railway. Discontinued with the parent train Apr 30 1971. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap, 2026-08-26: 383 points, 371.0 km / 230.5 mi total, of which Pasco - Vancouver is 220.1 mi against the 221 miles Wikipedia documents for the North Bank Road (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Portland_and_Seattle_Railway, "a 221-mile section from Pasco to Vancouver"), a 0.4% fit; the remaining 10.4 mi is Vancouver across the Columbia to Portland Union Station. No straight-line approximation anywhere: the trace is a continuous shortest path over the OSM way graph of BNSF's Fallbridge Subdivision (relation 1443651, Pasco - Vancouver - Portland, the ex-SP&S north bank main), plus the last 3.2 km into Pasco station from the Lakeside Subdivision (relation 1443649, the ex-SP&S Pasco - Spokane line, which shares its southern end node with the Fallbridge Sub). Largest gap between consecutive traced nodes is 2.9 km, in the open country south of Pasco where OSM node spacing is coarse - that is sparse mapping, not a bridged gap. Douglas-Peucker simplified at 25 m. CAVEAT, per Rule 2: this is today's alignment, not the 1908 one. Bonneville (1938), The Dalles (1957) and John Day (1968) dams raised the river over the north bank shelf and the railroad was relocated onto higher ground through each pool; the pre-dam line lay lower and closer to the water there. The size of that offset has not been measured here.

segments.note: Northern Pacific's original Puget Sound line, built mainly by Chinese laborers, reached Tacoma from Kalama on the Columbia River Dec 16 1873 -- the railroad's first arrival on the Sound. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: With no rail link onward, passengers and freight bound for Portland had to transfer at Kalama to steamers running down the Columbia and Willamette rivers. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: Northern Pacific closed the gap in 1884 by putting the 338-foot railcar ferry Kalama (soon renamed Tacoma) into service, carrying entire trains across the Columbia between Kalama, WA and Goble, OR, where the Oregon Railway and Navigation Company's line continued on to Portland; that same year, June 17 1884, NP also completed its first direct rail link from Tacoma north to Seattle. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

Hill's Spokane, Portland and Seattle Railway finished the first rail bridge across the Columbia between Vancouver, WA and Portland Nov 5 1908, finally giving Northern Pacific an all-rail Seattle-Portland route; the Kalama-Goble train ferry was discontinued the same year. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
